THE CLAIMTechnical report · Category 17 · August 2026

Feed law lets a complete pet food carry up to 5,000 µg/kg of lead and 2,000 µg/kg of cadmium. The human food it is made from is held to a small fraction of that. HMTc certifies pets to the human number.

## Abstract

A dog or a cat eats one manufactured food, from one recipe, every day for a decade or more. It is the closest thing in the household to an infant on formula: a sole-source diet, delivered to a small body, without the dietary variety that dilutes any single exposure. Yet the heavy-metal limits that govern that food are not the limits that govern food for people. Pet food is regulated as animal feed, and feed limits are written with a wide margin above the human-food maxima the same governments enforce. This briefing sets out what the published literature actually measures in commercial pet food, why each metal matters for a companion animal, and why the Heavy Metal Tested & Certified program certifies pet food to the stricter human-food limit rather than the feed floor it is legally allowed to meet.

## Two rulebooks for the same bowl In law, pet food is feed, not food. In the European Union it is governed by Directive 2002/32 on undesirable substances in animal feed; in the United States by the Food and Drug Administration's Center for Veterinary Medicine and the model regulations of the Association of American Feed Control Officials; and in the national instruments of exporting countries. Those frameworks set maximum levels for the same metals human-food law addresses, but at a different height. Directive 2002/32 permits a complete pet feed to contain lead up to 5,000 µg/kg, cadmium up to 2,000 µg/kg, and total arsenic up to 2,000 µg/kg on a 12-percent-moisture basis [6]. China's Hygienical Standard for Pet Feed sets lead at 5, cadmium at 2, chromium at 5, mercury at 0.3, and arsenic at 10 mg/kg [2]: the same lax band, expressed per kilogram. Japan's pet-food standard sits in the same range. The human-food maxima the same governments enforce are far lower. The European Union limits cadmium in meat to 50 µg/kg and in pulses to 40 µg/kg; Israel limits inorganic arsenic in meat to 20 µg/kg and lead in dairy to 20 µg/kg; the strictest national limits for lead in muscle meat sit near 100 µg/kg [7]. Between the feed ceiling a pet food may legally meet and the food ceiling its human-grade equivalent must meet lies a gap of ten to fifty times, and nothing in feed law asks a brand to close it. Two of these frameworks do not set numeric heavy-metal limits at all. AAFCO's model regulations and the National Research Council's nutrient guidelines are silent on chromium, nickel, and aluminium in pet food; a survey of forty-nine United States dry dog foods noted the absence of any AAFCO or NRC standard for these elements as an open regulatory gap [4]. Where the rulebook is silent, the only limit is the one a certifier chooses to impose. ## What the literature finds in the bowl The gap would be academic if commercial pet food were uniformly clean. The published record says otherwise, across every metal the program certifies. Lead is the clearest case, and the most vivid example comes from raw diets built on game meat. A 2023 study analysed commercial raw minced pheasant dog food sold by United Kingdom online retailers and found a weighted mean lead concentration of 221 mg/kg dry weight in samples known or assumed to be free of visible shot, roughly thirty-four times the level expected from background contamination alone [1]. Between two-thirds and all of the packages of three raw pheasant products exceeded the European maximum level for animal muscle, while tinned pheasant and every chicken product tested at zero exceedances. X-ray imaging found radio-dense fragments, embedded lead shot, in three-quarters to all of the raw pheasant packages, and ten percent still contained shot at the point of analysis after macroscopic removal. The same study found that pheasant sold for human consumption exceeded the European limit in sixty-nine percent of samples, which is exactly the point: a game-meat ingredient too contaminated for a person is not thereby fit for a dog. Arsenic and lead recur in broad market surveys. An analysis of 196 commercial pet-food products from Lebanon and the United Arab Emirates, measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, found lead and arsenic exceeding regulatory safety thresholds in a portion of the sampled foods, with the contamination distributed across both dry and wet formats [3]. A separate assessment of 93 imported cat and dog foods sold in Chinese supermarkets measured lead, cadmium, chromium, mercury, and arsenic in every sample and ran an acute hazard-index calculation for cats and dogs; the study reported measurable burdens of all five metals and higher mean lead and cadmium in cat food than in dog food [2]. Cadmium tracks the animal fraction. Organ meat, bone meal, and marine ingredients concentrate cadmium, and the surveys reflect it: the Lebanon and UAE study measured mean cadmium of 251 µg/kg in cat food against 112 µg/kg in dog food, a difference consistent with the higher marine and organ content of feline diets [3]. Both figures sit at or above the strictest human-food maximum for meat. Mercury is the metal that most distinguishes cat food. Fish and marine protein are staples of feline diets, and methylmercury biomagnifies up the aquatic food chain in a way it never does in terrestrial ingredients. The Chinese survey measured mercury across cat and dog foods against a pet-feed ceiling of 0.3 mg/kg [2]; the human-food limit for the fish those diets are built from is lower still, and it is the human limit, split into total and methylmercury, that a fish-based diet should answer to. Aluminium, nickel, and chromium are the metals the rulebook forgets. The survey of forty-nine United States dry dog foods found aluminium above the average human daily intake on a per-calorie basis in every product tested, and chromium and molybdenum above human intake as well, against no governing standard for any of them [4]. Finished treats carry the same elements: a study of nutraceutical dog snacks measured cadmium, lead, chromium, and nickel in extruded and dried prototypes [5], the product class a pet most often receives outside its measured daily ration. ## Why it lands harder on a dog or a cat Three features of companion-animal feeding turn a modest concentration into a meaningful dose. The diet is sole-source and lifelong, so there is no dietary variety to average an exposure down, and the exposure runs for the whole of a shorter life. Body mass is small, so a fixed concentration delivers a larger dose per kilogram than the same food would deliver to a person. And the toxic metals do not clear; lead deposits in bone, cadmium accumulates in the kidney over years, and methylmercury crosses into the nervous system. A pet is, in exposure terms, a small body on a formula diet, which is the population human-food law protects most stringently, not least. The species differ in ways the diet amplifies. Cats eat more fish and organ meat, which is where mercury and cadmium concentrate. Dogs on raw or game-based diets take on the lead burden of the meat's own contamination, as the pheasant data show. Neither animal chooses its food, varies it, or can be told to eat less of a bad lot; the entire margin of safety is set upstream, by whoever decides what the food is allowed to contain. ## The case for a human-grade standard The Heavy Metal Tested & Certified program resolves the two-rulebook problem in one direction only. For every pet-food subcategory and every metal, the standard is not the feed limit but the strictest maximum level a credible government sets for the nearest human food, adopted as a voluntary over-compliance and stated in the product's own basis. A dry complete diet is held to the strictest human limits for the cereals, pulses, and starchy tubers it is built from; a canned or raw diet to the human limits for meat; a fish-based diet to the human seafood limits, mercury split into both forms; a milk replacer to the human limits for dairy. The metals no government limits in any food, aluminium among them, are not left blank: they are measured on every lot as controls, and hexavalent chromium is treated as the measurement artifact it is, bounded by total chromium. The result is a standard that reads, cell by cell, as a deliberate step down from the feed floor. Where feed law permits 5,000 µg/kg of lead in a complete diet, the human-grade limit for dry pet food is 100; where it permits 2,000 µg/kg of cadmium, the human-grade limit is 40. Each of the ten subcategory standards discloses the feed floor beside the human number it is certified to, so the over-compliance is stated, not implied. That disclosure is the argument: a certified pet food is held to the maximum levels that govern food for people, and the gap it closes is written on the page. None of this rests on novel toxicology or on limits invented for the purpose. Every certified number is a sovereign human-food maximum already in force somewhere in the world, applied to a pet product by choice. The literature baseline for pet-food occurrence and for each metal is maintained independently at the [Heavy Metal Index](https://heavymetalindex.com); this program applies those findings, and the two are kept editorially separate by design. ## Frequently asked questions ### Is pet food regulated for heavy metals at all? Yes, but as animal feed rather than as food. The EU's Directive 2002/32, the FDA's Center for Veterinary Medicine, AAFCO's model regulations, and national pet-feed standards set maximum levels for several metals, generally far higher than the limits the same governments set for human food. Some metals, including chromium, nickel, and aluminium, are not addressed by AAFCO or NRC at all. ### What does “human-grade” heavy-metal certification mean here? For each pet-food subcategory and metal, HMTc certifies to the strictest maximum level a credible government sets for the nearest human food, not the laxer feed limit. The feed floor is disclosed beside every certified value so the voluntary over-compliance is visible. ### Which metals matter most in pet food? Lead in game-meat and raw diets, arsenic in grain- and rice-based diets, mercury in fish-based cat food, and cadmium in organ- and marine-heavy diets are the best-documented signals in the published surveys. Aluminium, nickel, and chromium recur in dry foods against no governing limit. ### Why are pets more exposed than people? A companion animal eats one manufactured diet for its whole life, has a small body mass that raises the dose per kilogram, and cannot vary its food. Lead, cadmium, and methylmercury accumulate rather than clear, so a lifelong sole-source diet concentrates the exposure. ## References

THE CLAIMTechnical report · HMTc Standards Briefing 10 · August 2026

A supplement is one of the few products a household shares across a fifty-kilogram difference in body weight. Its limits were written for the adult; the child eats from the same bottle. HMTc certifies every supplement to the limit that protects the child, and says what that costs.

## Abstract

A dietary supplement is one of the few consumer products a household shares across a fifty-kilogram difference in body weight: the gummy multivitamin, the greens powder, the protein, the syrup, the melatonin all cross the line between adult and child in ordinary use. The heavy-metal limits that govern these products were written for the adult. On a per-kilogram basis, a serving that clears an adult intake reference delivers four to five times that dose to a fifteen-kilogram child, and the child's developing system is the most sensitive to it.

HMTc responds by holding every certified supplement, adult-labeled or not, to the strictest maximum level any credible government sets for the metal in an infant-or-young-child food: lead at ten micrograms per kilogram against an adult supplement floor that begins at one thousand, cadmium at five against three hundred, inorganic arsenic a hundred and fifty times below the USP adult figure, and nickel, tin, and aluminium held at infant-food limits in a framework that sets no supplement limit for them at all. The over-compliance is stated plainly, including its cost to adult-only brands, because the shared bottle is the ordinary case and the child is the binding one.

## The dose that matters is per kilogram Toxicology does not care what a label says. It cares how much of a metal reaches a body relative to the size of that body. Lead, cadmium, and inorganic arsenic are dosed per kilogram of body weight, and the tolerable intakes the world's regulators publish are all expressed that way: micrograms per kilogram per day, or per week. A serving of a supplement delivers a fixed quantity of any contaminant it carries. That fixed quantity, divided into a fifteen-kilogram child, is four to five times the per-kilogram dose it delivers to a seventy-kilogram adult. The serving did not change. The label did not change. The exposure that the body actually experiences is several-fold higher, and it is higher precisely for the consumer whose developing nervous system is most sensitive to it. This is not a hypothetical about misuse. It is the arithmetic of a shared bottle, and it is why, across the food side of contaminant regulation, infant and young-child categories carry the strictest limits any government sets. The child is not an edge case to be warned away from the product. On a per-kilogram basis the child is the binding safety case, and a limit that does not protect the child does not protect the household. ## The floor was built for an adult Set against that, the framework that governs supplement composition is adult all the way down. In the United States the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, the statute that defines the category, sets no heavy-metal maximum at all; it is a marketing-and-manufacturing framework, not a contaminant standard. The pharmacopeial reference brands actually test against, USP General Chapter 2232, sets permitted daily exposures for lead, cadmium, inorganic arsenic, and mercury, and it computes every one of them for an adult consumer: five micrograms of lead a day, five of cadmium, fifteen of inorganic arsenic, fifteen of mercury [1]. Expressed as a concentration on USP's own assumption of a ten-gram daily serving, that is a lead limit of five hundred micrograms per kilogram. The food-supplement maximum levels that a handful of governments have published run laxer still: lead permitted at one thousand micrograms per kilogram in Thailand, three thousand across the Gulf states, Israel, and Vietnam, ten thousand in the ASEAN guideline and Singapore [2][3]. None of these numbers was set with a child's body weight in the denominator, because none of these instruments was written for a product a child would take. The one jurisdiction that has looked hardest at these metals shows the shape of the gap most clearly. California's Proposition 65 sets a developmental safe-harbour for lead of half a microgram a day, on the reproductive endpoint, a thousandfold below the observed-effect level [4]. That is the number a toxicologist reaches for when the exposed population includes the developing. It is ten times below the adult USP daily figure and it exists in the same state whose supplement aisles are stocked with products certified, if at all, against the adult one. The developmental science is already written down. It simply was never the number the supplement floor was built on. ## What HMTc holds every supplement to Faced with an adult floor and a child who eats from it, HMTc does not split the category into two tiers and certify children's products more tightly than adults'. It holds all of them to the child. For every supplement form and every ingredient class, the HMTc limit for each metal is the strictest maximum level any credible government has set for that metal in an infant-or-young-child food, converted to the supplement's own basis and applied without regard to how the product is labeled [5][6][7]. Lead is held at ten micrograms per kilogram, the strictest sovereign infant-formula lead maximum, against an adult supplement floor that begins at one thousand: a hundredfold difference. Cadmium is held at five, against an adult floor of three hundred. Inorganic arsenic is held at ten, a hundred and fifty times below the concentration USP's adult figure implies. Total mercury is held at four micrograms per kilogram, against adult supplement limits of one hundred to five hundred. The program adopts the child limit openly as a read-across and never as a government limit on the supplement itself, because no government sets an infant-food limit for an adult protein powder; HMTc chooses it, and says so. For three of the eight metals the over-compliance is not a matter of degree but of kind, because the adult framework sets no supplement limit at all. Nickel, tin, and aluminium have no dietary-supplement maximum in any of these regimes, and USP 2232 does not cover them. A conventional certificate is simply silent on them. HMTc holds nickel to one hundred micrograms per kilogram, the strictest infant-formula nickel maximum, in a category where a child already exceeds the tolerable nickel intake European regulators have set [8]; it holds aluminium to five hundred, the only government aluminium limit for any food in the world; and it treats any measurable tin on a non-canned supplement as a packaging signal to be investigated rather than a level to be permitted. Where the adult framework says nothing, the child-food limit is the whole of the standard. ## The classes where the line is hardest to hold Some supplement classes make this posture expensive, and those are exactly the ones where it matters most. Clay, mineral, and earth-derived products, bentonite and diatomaceous earth and zeolite and shilajit, are geological materials that carry lead and arsenic at concentrations the earth put there; shilajit in particular routinely tests well above every infant-food limit for both. Greens and superfood blends combine leaf, root, algae, and cereal-grass material selected, in effect, for the plant families that draw lead, cadmium, and inorganic arsenic out of soil most efficiently. Botanicals and traditional herbal formulas have a long documented association with lead and arsenic exposure. For every one of these classes the HMTc limit is the same strict child-food number as for a vitamin tablet. The program does not compute a looser limit from what these materials typically contain, because a standard that relaxed to meet the contamination it found would certify the contamination. The line is held, and where a class cannot meet it, the honest answer is that the class is not yet clean enough to carry the mark, not that the mark should move. ## The same rule, applied twice This is the second time the program has made this structural choice, and the two together are easier to defend than either alone. Pet food is governed by feed law, whose heavy-metal limits run looser than the limits for human food; HMTc certifies pets to the stricter human-food limit anyway, the decision set out in [the pet-food briefing](/briefings/heavy-metals-in-pet-food), because the animal does not choose what is put in its bowl. Supplements are governed by an adult framework; HMTc certifies them to the stricter child-food limit, because the child eats from the same bottle as the adult. Both are one rule applied twice: certify to the level that protects the most vulnerable consumer who will realistically use the product, and disclose the looser legal floor rather than shelter behind it. Naming the rule matters, because a certifier that keeps one protective bar across a whole category is doing something a certifier that lets its bar drift toward the least-protected buyer is not. The supplement decision is not an exception carved for one category; it is the same standard the program applies wherever the law protects the wrong person. ## The tradeoff, stated plainly Holding an adult supplement to a child's limit asks more of the brand than any government does. A protein or greens or mineral brand that has never sold a product for children, and never intends to, must nonetheless meet a bar built from infant-formula science to earn the certificate. That is a real cost and the program does not disguise it. What the brand receives for it is the only claim in the category that answers the question a parent actually has. A shelf full of supplements certified against adult limits tells a family nothing about the eight-year-old who eats the gummies. A supplement carrying the HMTc mark says that its contaminant load was measured against the level set to protect the most vulnerable person who will realistically consume it, and held there regardless of who the marketing was for. In a market where the product crosses the age line every day and the standards mostly do not, that is the difference worth certifying, and it is worth stating in exactly those terms. ## References

Works cited in this briefing’s text, in first-appearance order. This is not the full evidence base for the underlying standard; it is only what the prose above draws on. Every range in the briefing is a model built on one of these published anchors. Where a work carries a DOI or a public URL, its title and domain link to it; primary legal documents and published standards are named but not linked to a corpus record.

A dietary supplement is one of the few consumer products a family shares across a fifty-kilogram difference in body weight. The greens powder, the protein, the elderberry syrup, the melatonin, the children's chewable that is chemically the adult chewable at a lower count: all of them cross the line between adult and child in ordinary use, in ordinary homes, with no label instruction violated. It is the arithmetic of a shared bottle, and it is why, across the food side of contaminant regulation, infant and young-child categories carry the strictest limits any government sets. ## The floor was built for an adult

Set against that, the framework that governs supplement composition is adult all the way down. In the United States the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, the statute that defines the category, sets no heavy-metal maximum at all; it is a marketing-and-manufacturing framework, not a contaminant standard. The pharmacopeial reference brands actually test against, USP General Chapter 2232, sets permitted daily exposures for lead, cadmium, inorganic arsenic, and mercury, and it computes every one of them for an adult consumer: five micrograms of lead a day, five of cadmium, fifteen of inorganic arsenic, fifteen of mercury [1]. Expressed as a concentration on USP's own assumption of a ten-gram daily serving, that is a lead limit of five hundred micrograms per kilogram. The food-supplement maximum levels that a handful of governments have published run laxer still: lead permitted at one thousand micrograms per kilogram in Thailand, three thousand across the Gulf states, Israel, and Vietnam, ten thousand in the ASEAN guideline and Singapore [2][3]. None of these numbers was set with a child's body weight in the denominator, because none of these instruments was written for a product a child would take.

The one jurisdiction that has looked hardest at these metals shows the shape of the gap most clearly. California's Proposition 65 sets a developmental safe-harbour for lead of half a microgram a day, on the reproductive endpoint, a thousandfold below the observed-effect level [4]. That is the number a toxicologist reaches for when the exposed population includes the developing. It is ten times below the adult USP daily figure and it exists in the same state whose supplement aisles are stocked with products certified, if at all, against the adult one. The developmental science is already written down. It simply was never the number the supplement floor was built on.

## What HMTc holds every supplement to

Faced with an adult floor and a child who eats from it, HMTc does not split the category into two tiers and certify children's products more tightly than adults'. It holds all of them to the child. For every supplement form and every ingredient class, the HMTc limit for each metal is the strictest maximum level any credible government has set for that metal in an infant-or-young-child food, converted to the supplement's own basis and applied without regard to how the product is labeled [5][6][7]. Lead is held at ten micrograms per kilogram, the strictest sovereign infant-formula lead maximum, against an adult supplement floor that begins at one thousand: a hundredfold difference. Cadmium is held at five, against an adult floor of three hundred. Inorganic arsenic is held at ten, a hundred and fifty times below the concentration USP's adult figure implies. Total mercury is held at four micrograms per kilogram, against adult supplement limits of one hundred to five hundred. The program adopts the child limit openly as a read-across and never as a government limit on the supplement itself, because no government sets an infant-food limit for an adult protein powder; HMTc chooses it, and says so.

For three of the eight metals the over-compliance is not a matter of degree but of kind, because the adult framework sets no supplement limit at all. Nickel, tin, and aluminium have no dietary-supplement maximum in any of these regimes, and USP 2232 does not cover them. A conventional certificate is simply silent on them. HMTc holds nickel to one hundred micrograms per kilogram, the strictest infant-formula nickel maximum, in a category where a child already exceeds the tolerable nickel intake European regulators have set [8]; it holds aluminium to five hundred, the only government aluminium limit for any food in the world; and it treats any measurable tin on a non-canned supplement as a packaging signal to be investigated rather than a level to be permitted. Where the adult framework says nothing, the child-food limit is the whole of the standard.

## The classes where the line is hardest to hold

Some supplement classes make this posture expensive, and those are exactly the ones where it matters most. Clay, mineral, and earth-derived products, bentonite and diatomaceous earth and zeolite and shilajit, are geological materials that carry lead and arsenic at concentrations the earth put there; shilajit in particular routinely tests well above every infant-food limit for both. Greens and superfood blends combine leaf, root, algae, and cereal-grass material selected, in effect, for the plant families that draw lead, cadmium, and inorganic arsenic out of soil most efficiently. Botanicals and traditional herbal formulas have a long documented association with lead and arsenic exposure. For every one of these classes the HMTc limit is the same strict child-food number as for a vitamin tablet. The program does not compute a looser limit from what these materials typically contain, because a standard that relaxed to meet the contamination it found would certify the contamination. The line is held, and where a class cannot meet it, the honest answer is that the class is not yet clean enough to carry the mark, not that the mark should move.

## The same rule, applied twice

This is the second time the program has made this structural choice, and the two together are easier to defend than either alone. Pet food is governed by feed law, whose heavy-metal limits run looser than the limits for human food; HMTc certifies pets to the stricter human-food limit anyway, the decision set out in [the pet-food briefing](/briefings/heavy-metals-in-pet-food), because the animal does not choose what is put in its bowl. Supplements are governed by an adult framework; HMTc certifies them to the stricter child-food limit, because the child eats from the same bottle as the adult. Both are one rule applied twice: certify to the level that protects the most vulnerable consumer who will realistically use the product, and disclose the looser legal floor rather than shelter behind it. Naming the rule matters, because a certifier that keeps one protective bar across a whole category is doing something a certifier that lets its bar drift toward the least-protected buyer is not. The supplement decision is not an exception carved for one category; it is the same standard the program applies wherever the law protects the wrong person.

## The tradeoff, stated plainly

Holding an adult supplement to a child's limit asks more of the brand than any government does. A protein or greens or mineral brand that has never sold a product for children, and never intends to, must nonetheless meet a bar built from infant-formula science to earn the certificate. That is a real cost and the program does not disguise it. What the brand receives for it is the only claim in the category that answers the question a parent actually has. A shelf full of supplements certified against adult limits tells a family nothing about the eight-year-old who eats the gummies. A supplement carrying the HMTc mark says that its contaminant load was measured against the level set to protect the most vulnerable person who will realistically consume it, and held there regardless of who the marketing was for. In a market where the product crosses the age line every day and the standards mostly do not, that is the difference worth certifying, and it is worth stating in exactly those terms.
